subject_area: Computer security — principles, management, and defensive controls
course_intent: Teach the principles and practices of computer security across access control, risk management, intrusion detection, and related defensive controls — students should leave able to explain core security mechanisms, identify threats, and reason about how organizations select and deploy controls to protect IT assets.
depth_bound: Recommendations stay at the conceptual + mechanism level grounded in standards (NIST, ISO 27000, RFCs) and canonical examples (UNIX permissions, Snort rules, RBAC/ABAC models). Hands-on exploit development, deep cryptographic math, secure-coding labs in specific languages, and red-team penetration walkthroughs are beyond this course's depth bound.
key_topics: Access control models (DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC) and access matrix
UNIX file access control with traditional permissions and ACLs
RBAC reference models (RBAC0–RBAC3), role hierarchies, and constraints
IT security management process and ISO 27000 / NIST SP 800 standards
Security risk assessment approaches (baseline, informal, formal, combined)
Intruder classification, skill levels, and attack methodology stages
Intrusion detection systems (HIDS, NIDS, distributed/hybrid IDS)
Honeypots (low- vs high-interaction) and deployment locations
Snort architecture and rule format for network intrusion detection
one_liner: Undergraduate computer-security fundamentals covering access control models, IT security management/risk assessment, intruder behavior, and intrusion detection systems at a principles-and-mechanisms level — does NOT include hands-on exploitation labs, cryptographic deep dives, or framework-specific secure-coding tutorials.
